text_blocks.snippet: U.S. immigration policy is largely defined by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which governs both the admission of immigrants and immigration enforcement. Key aspects include family-based and employment-based immigration, refugee and asylum provisions, and various temporary visa categories. The system also involves enforcement measures, including border control and deportation.
snippet_highlighted_words: largely defined by the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), which governs both the admission of immigrants and immigration enforcement

text_blocks.snippet: Key Components of U.S. Immigration Policy:

list.title: INA:
list.snippet: The primary law governing immigration, outlining categories for lawful permanent residence and other statuses.

list.title: Family-based immigration:
list.snippet: Allows U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents to sponsor certain family members for permanent residence.

list.title: Employment-based immigration:
list.snippet: Offers pathways for skilled workers and professionals to obtain green cards.

list.title: Refugee and asylum provisions:
list.snippet: Provides protection for individuals fleeing persecution or violence.

list.title: Temporary visas:
list.snippet: Various nonimmigrant visas for students, tourists, workers, and others.

list.title: Enforcement and removal:
list.snippet: Includes border control, detention, and deportation of individuals not authorized to be in the U.S.

list.title: Diversity Immigrant Visa Program:
list.snippet: Grants green cards to individuals from countries with low rates of immigration to the U.S.

list.title: DACA (Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals):
list.snippet: A program that provides temporary protection from deportation and work permits to certain unauthorized immigrants who arrived in the U.S. as children.

list.title: TPS (Temporary Protected Status):
list.snippet: Provides temporary protection from deportation to individuals from designated countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disasters, or other extraordinary conditions.

list.title: Backlogs and Processing Times:
list.snippet: Significant backlogs exist in both family and employment-based immigration, leading to lengthy waiting periods for visas and green cards.

list.title: Enforcement Priorities:
list.snippet: Recent administrations have focused on increased border security and interior enforcement, including detention and deportation.

list.title: Policy Debates:
list.snippet: Immigration policy remains a contentious issue, with debates surrounding border security, pathways to citizenship, and the treatment of unauthorized immigrants.
